## Introduction

RESY implements the **Expert System (ESy)** framework for vegetation
classification (Bruelheide [1997](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02803883); Chytrý et al. [2020](https://doi.org/10.1111/avsc.12519)).
An ESy file encodes three sections:

1. **Taxonomy** – species aggregations and synonyms  
2. **Taxon groups** – species assemblages referenced in classification conditions  
3. **Vegetation types** – logical formulas that combine group thresholds into
   named habitat types

The package can work with any ESy-compliant classification. This vignette uses
two bundled systems:

- **EUNIS** (European Nature Information System habitat types;
  [FloraVeg.EU](https://floraveg.eu/habitat/))
- **Apennine-test** (a simplified test system for the Italian Apennines)

Many EUNIS rules also use site data from the header table (`Ecoreg`,
`Country`, `Coast_EEA`, `Dunes_Bohn`). `vignette("EUNIS")` shows how to add
these columns.

```{r libraries, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(RESY)
```

---

## 1. Load and prepare species data

`resy_classify()` expects the observation table to have one row per species in
each plot, with three columns. Each column can also have its
[Darwin Core](https://dwc.tdwg.org/) name, the standard set of field names for
biodiversity data:

| Column | Darwin Core name | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `PlotObservationID` | `eventID` | Plot identifier |
| `TaxonName` | `scientificName` | Species name |
| `Cover_Perc` | `organismQuantity`, with `organismQuantityType` `"% cover"` | Cover of the species in percent |

For a species column with any other name, set `species_col`. The example data
uses `scientificName`.

```{r load-species, message=FALSE}
data_species <- read_csv(
  system.file("extdata", "data_example_species.csv", package = "RESY"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

glimpse(data_species)
```

The **header** table has one row per plot, with the plot ID and the site data
the rules use, such as the country or the altitude. `Apennine-test` uses no site
data, so here the header table contains only the plot IDs, but
`resy_classify()` still requires it. It must contain the same plot ID column as
the observation table.

```{r header}
header <- data_species |>
  distinct(PlotObservationID) |>
  as.data.frame()
```

---

## 2. Load expert systems

`resy_available_classifications()` lists the schemes and versions bundled with the package.

```{r available}
resy_available_classifications() |> select(scheme, version)
```

To add your own expert system, use `resy_add_classification()`.

`resy_load_expert()` reads a bundled expert system into a `resy_parsed_expert`
object, which the taxonomy check below uses. `resy_classify()` does not need
this object: it loads the expert system itself from `scheme` and `version`.

```{r load-experts}
parsed_apennine <- resy_load_expert(scheme = "Apennine-test")
```

The types of an expert system form a hierarchy. `resy_expert_tree()` prints it;
`fill = TRUE` adds the group levels that the type codes imply but the expert
system does not list:

```{r tree}
tree_filled <- resy_expert_tree(parsed_apennine, fill = TRUE)
print(tree_filled)
```

`Apennine-test` has two top-level types, forest (`F`) and non-forest (`N`),
each with lower-level types. To browse the hierarchy in the browser, use
`resy_view_expert()`.


## 3. Check taxonomy

`resy_check_taxonomy()` checks the species names of the observation table
against the species list of the expert system, including its synonyms. Each
expert system has its own list, so a name can match in one system and not in
another. The result has one row per distinct name: `scientificName` is the name as submitted, `TaxonName` the canonical name
the classifier uses (`NA` when unmatched), and `matched` whether it was found.
Printing it lists what each column holds and how many names matched.


```{r taxonomy-apennine}
tax_apennine <- resy_check_taxonomy(obs = data_species, parsed = parsed_apennine)
tax_apennine
```

`summary()` gives the match counts and lists the names that did not match:

```{r taxonomy-summary}
summary(tax_apennine)
```


## 4. Classify

`resy_classify()` evaluates the rules of every type for every plot and returns
a `resy_result` object. `scheme` selects the bundled expert system.

```{r classify-apennine, message=FALSE}
res_apennine <- resy_classify(
  obs    = data_species,
  header = header,
  scheme = "Apennine-test"
)
```

Each plot is assigned to one type. `resy_candidates()` with `wide = TRUE` gives
one row per plot; counting its `classification` column shows how many plots
went to each type:

```{r classification-counts}
cand_wide <- resy_candidates(res_apennine, wide = TRUE)
table(cand_wide$classification)
```

A plot marked `?` meets no type's rule and is not classified. Here, 92 of the
200 plots remain unclassified. In these plots, all four indicator groups have at
most 4% cover, below the lowest threshold in the rules (5%).

---

## 5. Inspect results

### Candidate types for all plots

A plot often meets the rules of several types, for example a lower-level type
and its parent. Each type has a priority in the expert system, and the plot is
assigned to the type with the highest priority. `resy_candidates()` lists every
type whose rule a plot meets, highest priority first. `priority_rank` numbers
the priority levels of the expert system from the lowest upward. Use `top_n` to
limit the number of types returned per plot.

```{r candidates-apennine}
cand_apennine <- resy_candidates(res_apennine, top_n = 3)
head(cand_apennine)
```

### Plot-level details

`resy_eval_plot()` prints the full evidence for one plot: its species, which
vegetation-type formulas evaluated to `TRUE`, and the type it is classified as.
It then lists the lower-level types the plot did not reach, with the result of
each of their conditions, which shows why the classification stopped at this
level.

```{r eval-plot}
# Replace "AN57" with a PlotObservationID present in your data
resy_eval_plot(res_apennine, p = "AN57")
```

Passing `type` explains any other type in the same way, whether or not its
rule holds for the plot:

```{r eval-plot-type}
resy_eval_plot(res_apennine, p = "AN57", type = "FB")
```

## Next steps

The classification above used an expert system without site data and species
names that already match it. With your own plots, one of these usually comes
next:

- **Your plots have coordinates and you want EUNIS habitat types:**
  `vignette("EUNIS")` adds the ecoregion, country and coastal position from the
  coordinates and classifies the plots.
- **Your species names follow another taxonomy**, such as GBIF or World Flora
  Online, and `resy_check_taxonomy()` reports many unmatched names:
  `vignette("taxonomy")` matches them to the names of the expert system.
- **Your plots have no altitude:** `vignette("altitude-vignette")` takes the
  altitude that some EUNIS rules use from a separately downloaded elevation map.
- **You have your own expert system:** `resy_validate_esy()` checks the file,
  and `resy_add_classification()` makes it available to `resy_classify()`.
